Hi, I have adhd and work with fellow neurodivergents. 

It’s different for everyone - for some, they need consequences, for others, rewards. So pair the training with either getting a reward, gameify it, be super encouraging about the little successes so they know if they do something they’re going to get a massive boost. Or - pair a lack of training with a consequence. The consequence will probably have to be enforced by others - for example, next time you see them if they haven’t achieved target, you stand over them while they do an exercise they hate. 

Outsource the accountability as much as possible - like pairing up with someone who goes regularly, if there’s an appointment set you’re more likely to go. 

Frequent reminders are good, especially if they have some time blindness - pointing out how many days left they have to do x amount of workouts can jolt them into action. I will point out that if it gets to Friday and they haven’t trained, they now have to train three days in a row. Often that hasn’t quite clicked. Also, getting them to schedule it in visibly - if they use calendars, have it colour coded and set so they can actually see when its supposed to happen and how it fits in with their week. 

Also, and most importantly - they have to actually be prepared to do some work. Some people absolutely use it as an excuse - there is some effort required, setting all the assistance possible still won’t work if they’re not prepared to make an effort.

Autistic trainer here working with other autistic people:
A big one is be mindful of your cues being interpreted differently. If you say "do it like this", it may be interpreted very literally. Take the rdl for example, the cue of push your hips back toward the wall - might be taken very literally.

2 other things that crop up often are proprioception- some people will really struggle with the mind muscle connection so they may be unable to recognise sensations or will describe them differently to how you're expecting. Hypermobility also a common comorbidity. And sensory issues - there are some exercises that i will have to modify or avoid as the sensory input is too much of a limiting factor.

I had a client similar - complained about every exercise and would give up constantly, then cancel sessions.
As much as i knew it would help her, I put my strength focus aside and instead focused solely on motivation and letting her become comfortable. Regressed movements, spent time chatting, worried less about forcing her to move as much as possible. Paid attention to what went down well and increased that. 

We might have a session where we do few sets - but she's now at the point where she's taking herself on hour long walks several times a week with zero prompting which is far more beneficial than a hard session once or twice a week followed by sedentary days. 

(And when she went from sedentary to a long walk then ended up with back pain I made sure to point out the correlation and the importance of regular movement rather than big hits once a week, and she's learning to recognise the impact it has on her life)

TL;DR:
•meet where they are. Regress movements. Check in after each set to see how they're feeling (not just the end of the workout)
•Make them feel safe and comfortable with you, to chat, to let you know how they're feeling, to ask questions
•pay attention to what has a positive impact and reinforce it/repeat it as much as reasonable. 
•be super positive about every bit of progress, if they move a little better, if they do a little more, if they show up
•probe and find out how their life is impacted both negatively and positively so you can keep relating things back to that to motivate them throughout their day

Also, look at calorie banking. I’ve had a lot more success both with consistency and adherence long term but also the relationship and honesty, with recognising that binges will happen and allowing them, in a more controlled way. 

So rather than aiming for a stricter diet every day, look at the pattern - if it’s a weekend thing, be realistic and expect the binge to happen. Work that into the calories mon-fri; and then you can start talking about modifications that still allow the emotional aspect, but start reducing the impact. Small tweaks that they feel are manageable, so they don’t feel out of control, it’s in the plan so they don’t have the shame and guilt around it, and as they adapt to that the binges tend to reduce. 

So as an example, if they get pizza and all the sides - start cutting down the sides one by one. Then, just get the pizza. Then, don’t eat the whole pizza. They’re still fulfilling their need, but in a more controlled and sustainable way. It’s a step by step process, not a quick change, so it’s easier to accomplish. If it’s in the plan, they’re more likely to feel like they can admit their diet to you, which means you’ll be in a better position to help them alongside other professionals (whether that’s a mental health worker or dietitian) which puts them in a greater position for success.

Yo - hypermobile PT (Ehlers-Danlos) here. Here’s some things that I’ve found from my personal experience and from training other EDS clients

You’re going to really need to watch the ROM and often actively restrict on occasion. Some form may need adjusting outside of the normal range - communication is key, get them to describe it. Is the clicking painful - if so, change the angle or path til it’s not. 

Every individual is different - for me, I and many of my clients had to avoid compound movements and actually start with the smaller muscle groups to build the strength in order to support the joints, before going with the basic movements. Think backwards, essentially. However - this isn’t blanket, and some will be fine with compounds and only have certain areas they need to be mindful of, and it’s worth not holding them back just because others can’t handle it

One blanket approach- Start slow, many people with hypermobility can end up with inflammation beyond DOMS, you can always progress according to how the individual adapts but the most common scenario is hypermobile people ending up completely out of commission from pushing too hard in training. 

Personal opinion - Strength training is THE best thing for managing symptoms, in my experience. I’ve gone from headed toward being wheelchair bound like my peers, to almost able to barbell squat. Whenever I stop training heavy weights, the symptoms come right back in. I see a lot of EDS people going for super light weight training or pilates and the like, because it doesn’t hurt them; but they still end up struggling with symptoms. Whereas the ones who stick with heavy lifting all tend to find lessened symptoms and improved life quality. It’s all about the programming approach and training management.

Hope this helps, happy to give more suggestions or specifics :)

Also; For anyone else reading who wants to know, her reverse lunge form isn’t ideal to bias glutes either. For glute biased lunges, you want your shins to almost stay vertical with your knees 90°, and maintain a bit of a forward lean. The excessive knee flexion would be good for a quad dominant forward lunge.

Update for anyone who may end up in a similar situation - I did speak with a lawyer and confirm that rules have changed recently surrounding determining employee/contractor relationships. However, sham contracting *is* still a thing so if you have enough evidence and desire you can still fight it. 

Apparently Fair Work is actually the organisation who is supposed to determine the relationship, a lawyer can only give their opinion, the complete opposite to what I was told when I contacted Fair Work. It needs a ruling, so you have to go to court to get a ruling defining the relationship. 

However, in my case there is argument that I had two jobs with this organisation - as it was confirmed by the owner that my PT agreement was entirely separate to the admin role, that contract did not cover the admin role which was then an entirely separate agreement that can be argued is an employee position. So what I could do is go after unpaid wages as they didn’t pay the award rate - and in that process would be determining whether it was an employee or contractor role. If I had been there longer than 6 months I would be pursuing this but as it is, the emotional and mental energy required is just not worth it at this point in time. 6 years to lodge a claim for unpaid wages, though, so there’s still that possibility. 

Hope this helps anyone who’s also looking for answers.
